title: Night prayer
hookLine: the short prayer before sleep, with the Nunc Dimittis of Simeon
carry: now let your servant go in peace

cards: The lights go down in a monastery chapel. The day's work is over, the last guests have gone, and the monks file in for one more short hour of prayer before bed.

It's gentle, almost a lullaby: a look back over the day, a psalm about resting under God's wings, a few lines of reading. And it ends with a man in the Temple, holding a baby, saying he can go in peace.
Then the lights go out, and nobody speaks until morning. Today's word is that last hour.

teach.b: Compline comes from the Latin completorium, the completing: the hour that finishes the day. First, the shape. It begins by looking back.
In today's Liturgy of the Hours there's a short examination of conscience: what did today hold, what do I regret, what am I grateful for.

teach.h: LOOK BACK, A PSALM, INTO THY HANDS.
teach.b: Then a psalm or two; on Sundays, Psalm 90 in the Douay numbering, the psalm about resting in the shadow of the Most High. Then a short reading, and a response taken from the psalms: into thy hands I commend my spirit.
In Luke, Jesus says that line on the cross. Said at bedtime, the echo is hard to miss.
Second, the song at its heart: the canticle of Simeon, from Luke's Gospel. Mary and Joseph bring the infant Jesus to the Temple.
A just and devout man named Simeon had been promised he wouldn't die before he saw the Christ.
He takes the baby in his arms and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace; because my eyes have seen thy salvation."
In Latin it begins Nunc dimittis, now you dismiss, and that's its name. Third, why at night. Simeon is ready to let go.
He's seen what he waited for, and he can rest.

teach.h: A DAILY PRACTICE OF LETTING GO.
teach.b: The Church sets his words at the edge of sleep, a small daily practice of letting go.

teach.h: NOW THOU DOST DISMISS THY SERVANT, O LORD.
teach.b: Fourth, the close: a hymn to Mary, often the Salve Regina, and then the house keeps silence until morning.

how: Monks and nuns pray Compline together before the night silence, and other Catholics pray it alone from a breviary or an app; it includes an examination of conscience, psalms, a short reading, the Nunc Dimittis and a closing antiphon to Mary.

o: a long vigil of prayer kept through the night
the short last prayer of the day, before sleep
a word of praise said after the evening meal

games.q: what's inside the hour — tap the pairs.
p: held the infant Jesus in the Temple
said on the cross, and before sleep

s: Compline is only for monks and priests
it took shape in monasteries, but laypeople pray it before bed too.
the song of Simeon comes from Luke's Gospel
Simeon holds the infant Jesus in the Temple and says he can now go in peace.
Compline is a long vigil through the night
it's short, and the night silence follows it.

games.q: you're Simeon. you were promised you'd see the Christ before you died, and now a young couple hands you their baby. what do you say?
o: ask God for more years to watch him grow.
say you can go now in peace, because you've seen it.
say nothing, and hand him back.
games.why: "now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace." he's ready to let go, and the Church sings his words every night.

practice: Look back over today, quickly and kindly: one thing you regret, one thing you're grateful for. Then, if you pray, say Simeon's words slowly: Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace.
If you don't pray, picture Simeon handing the baby back, and let your own day be handed back too.

wordCard.voice: Compline. From the Latin for completing: the last hour of the Church's day, prayed before sleep, with the song of Simeon at its heart. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: now you dismiss. the first words of Simeon's song in the Latin Bible, and its name.

carryVoice: Your line: now let your servant go in peace. A finished day can be let go. Day two hundred forty-one, and good night.
